explanations.explanation: Annas it is, friend. He's Caiaphas's father-in-law, so the family tree is doing some work in this story. The text says they bring Jesus to him first, before anyone else. I know a few things about being passed from one desk to the next, but that's another story.

Herod is a name from other accounts of the trial (Luke 23:7), but John doesn't bring him in here. In this passage the soldiers take Jesus first to Annas, the father-in-law of Caiaphas, the high priest that year. Easy name to grab, though. Plenty of names are flying around this night.

Pilate, the governor (Matthew 27:2), does show up in the story, but not yet. John 18:13 says they bring Jesus first to Annas, the father-in-law of Caiaphas. Pilate is farther down the road. Keep him in your back pocket, friend.

explanations.answer: It would be better if one man died for the people
explanations.explanation: That's the advice, word for word from the text. Caiaphas said it would be better if one man died for the people. Notice he said "died." That one word makes this a heavy line, and I think it's worth slowing down for.

explanations.answer: It would be better if one man ruled the people
explanations.explanation: Ruling would be a much nicer piece of advice, friend. But John 18:14 says Caiaphas advised that it would be better if one man died for the people. That word "died" is the heart of it. This is a heavy part of the story.

explanations.answer: It would be better if one man spoke for the people
explanations.explanation: Speaking for the people sounds like a good job for a spokesman. Not this time, though. The text says Caiaphas advised the Jews that it would be better if one man died for the people. That's a serious line, and John puts it right there.

True, baker. The other disciple goes in with Jesus because the high priest knows him. Peter stays outside at the door. He's standing out there like someone who showed up to the party without the invite.
This one's false, friend. The text says the other disciple goes into the courtyard of the high priest, but Peter stands outside at the door. He's not inside yet. Someone has to come and get him.
Peter answers, "I am not." That's a short answer to a short question, and it's a hard one to read. I think this is where the story gets heavy. Hold on to it, friend, because it comes back.

I wish that's how it went, friend. But the servant girl asks, "Aren't you also one of this man's disciples?" and the text says Peter answers, "I am not." It's a tough moment to read. I think it's a heavy one.

Silence would at least be quiet, but the text says Peter answers her. Her question is whether he's also one of this man's disciples, and he says, "I am not." That's a hard line to hear. Papa Dorin gets a little quiet here too.

Cold is right, friend. The text says that because it was cold, the servants and officers made a charcoal fire to keep warm. Peter's standing with them, warming himself. A fire on a cold night is the oldest idea there is.
A crowd might be around, but that's not the reason the text gives. It says they made the charcoal fire because it was cold. The fire is for keeping warm. It's not a crowd control strategy.

Nobody lights a fire to fix quiet, friend. A fire fixes cold, and cold is the reason the text gives. The servants and officers made a charcoal fire to keep warm. If I want quiet, I just turn off the mixer.
Teaching, yes. The high priest asks Jesus about His disciples and His teaching. Two things are on the table. Jesus answers right away, so listen to that next.

Miracles are a big part of the Gospels, but they're not on the list here. The text says the high priest questions Jesus about His disciples and His teaching. So the questions stay on who follows Him and what He taught.
Nobody asks about the family reunion in this passage. The high priest questions Jesus about His disciples and His teaching. That's the whole list, friend. Honest answer, short list.
Yes, friend. Jesus says, "Ask those who heard My message. Surely they know what I said." He taught openly, so there were plenty of people to ask. He doesn't point the high priest to anyone in secret.
Jesus doesn't send the high priest to the soldiers. He says, "Ask those who heard My message." The people to ask are the ones who sat there and listened. The soldiers were busy tying knots.

The teachers of the law don't come up in this exchange. Jesus tells the high priest, "Ask those who heard My message. Surely they know what I said." He means the people who were in the synagogues and at the temple. Anyone who was there can tell it.

explanations.answer: He asks why He was struck if He spoke correctly
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jesus replies, "If I said something wrong, testify as to what was wrong. But if I spoke correctly, why did you strike Me?" It's a plain, steady question. No yelling and no pleading. This is a heavy moment, and Jesus meets it calmly.

explanations.answer: He stays silent and looks away from him
explanations.explanation: The text says Jesus replied, so He doesn't stay silent. He answers, "If I said something wrong, testify as to what was wrong. But if I spoke correctly, why did you strike Me?" It's a hard scene to watch. I think it hurts, and I'm glad you're paying attention to what He actually said.

explanations.answer: He asks the high priest to have him removed
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't ask for anyone to be removed. He answers the officer directly: "If I said something wrong, testify as to what was wrong. But if I spoke correctly, why did you strike Me?" He asks the officer to show what was wrong, or to say why he struck Him. This is a heavy scene, friend.

I know you want a good ending for Peter, friend. The text doesn't give it yet. When they ask him if he's one of Jesus' disciples, he denies it and says, "I am not." This is a hard stretch, so I'll say it once: it's heavy.
False, baker. They ask him, "Aren't you also one of His disciples?" and he denies it. He says, "I am not." It's a heavy moment, and the text doesn't hide it.

Right away, a rooster crows. The text says Peter denied it once more, and immediately the rooster crowed. Jesus had told Peter earlier that the rooster wouldn't crow before Peter denied Him three times (John 13:38). That's a sound Peter was not expecting to hear.

The fire is still burning as far as the text says. It never mentions it going out. What happens right after Peter denies it once more is that a rooster crows. It's one loud sound in the early morning, and it matters.

The servant girl already did her part back at the door. This time the text says Peter denied it once more, and immediately a rooster crowed. No shouting is mentioned. Just a rooster, and it says plenty.
